content: // Model Carving // This work from Harvard and NYU proposes Model Carving, which puts a learnable scalar gate on every attention and MLP sublayer. The training loss closes gates it does not need, and those sublayers are removed. At equal training compute, carved models reached lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7x more compute. They tested standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers up to 1.3B. Carved models also beat size-matched models made by pruning or distillation. The advantage grew with scale and held on few-shot evaluation and generation. Removed sublayers do not run, so carved models used up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decoded up to 1.6x faster with no quality loss. If you need a small model for edge or latency-bound use, compare carving during pretraining against your current prune-then-distill pipeline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27962 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/model-carving-training-transformers-that-optimize-their-own-topology-2611.27962

My hot take: we already have enough raw infrastructure to withstand all of the most adverse structural headwinds. AI models are now powerful enough to optimize the living daylights out of the current compute. I should know, I’ve been doing it on a string budget for months. That, in turn, will lead to even more powerful AI. All of which assumes we don’t get *any* major algorithmic breakthroughs for better AI models themselves, which is extremely implausible. In other words, there is no putting this genie back in the bottle. What matters is not Mr. Huang’s libido; what matters is that the technological revolution of artificial intelligence is running into powerful, structural headwinds: rising short- and long-term interest rates, a major political backlash, and an intensification of Cold War II.

Yeah, all those headwinds suck, and are going to mess things up in substantive ways for all of us in the coming couple of years. But in terms of AI development it will be just an extremely minor inconvenience. I mean, the current trajectory is already hyperexponential, so the worst case scenario is we still get an exponential growth.

Banger paper from MIT CSAIL. (bookmark it) It discusses how harnesses can generalize compositionality. In other words, harnesses can push LLMs further (with stronger generalization effects) through existing LLM capabilities. There is a huge debate on whether models will eat harnesses, but this work shows the power of custom harnesses and why they will continue to matter. Standard harnesses keep adding to the context, so the model has to handle inputs unlike anything it trained on. An RLM harness manages context in code and splits a task so each model call sees a familiar input, even when the full task is new. Under RL, RLMs trained only on short tasks generalized to tasks 2 to 64 times longer, and training on one domain transferred to new domains with shared structure. For complex tasks, they train individual calls inside the harness on easier synthetic environments with fake tools and sub-calls. They call this surrogate harness training. RLM-27B, trained this way on synthetic data, improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same harness by 26.9% on average on hard long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench, with about 2 times fewer tokens. If long trajectories are expensive to train on, try training the individual calls inside your harness on short synthetic tasks first. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28298 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/language-model-harnesses-can-be-compositional-generalizers-2611.28298

This is a fascinating research topic and matters a lot in a world of RSI. It investigated whether an LLM can tell from the first 20% of a training run how it will end. The strongest LLMs can. They match or beat dedicated curve-fitting methods, but only when the run is logged in detail. Researchers built Tea Leaves from 682 real runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and RL. The forecaster sees the config, description, code, and early curve, then predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs, the strongest matched the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and led on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). More information helped more than more effort. Related runs in the prompt cut loss-curve error by 39%, while tools added little. On sparsely logged runs, every method lost most of its skill. A small open model trained on public runs matched the best LLM on loss curves. Research agents today train every run to the end. Log densely, give your agent related runs, and use its forecasts to rank which runs get more compute. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30141 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/reading-the-tea-leaves-again-can-large-language-models-predict-language-model-tr-2611.30141

In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history. You can read the full post here: https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images. With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found. I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history. I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the sketchbook. The itinerary also aligned perfectly with the few dated drawings in the book. But there was actually the type of conclusive evidence we rarely get as historians: on 18 June 1808, after Chabot’s canoe reached Fort St. Joseph, he wrote “I took a sketch” before describing the exact view of the fort depicted in a matching drawing. The journal itself is also a major find. It had been mentioned once in a dissertation footnote, but in a completely different area of history and is unknown to fur trade or Canadian historians. It’s long and detailed, covering some 162 notebook pages which makes this a significant new document to my field. Attached to the journal was another trove of documents too: excerpts from long-destroyed North West Company papers, journals, and letters. Again, this almost never happens. Both finds equally surprised the other leading experts I consulted. Although we can construct a coherent narrative in hindsight, I cannot emphasize enough how exceedingly difficult this sort of thinking and recall is for humans. Unlike a human, Astra was able to tackle the problem from both ends at once: working forward from the scant facts of the 1808 journey pictured in the sketchbook and backwards from the immense number of surviving facts about 1808 British North America in general. While we can technically explain Astra’s path to this find as a product of enhanced search capabilities, it conducted the investigation from end to end. I basically acted as the research assistant, restricting copies of the paper documents it needed. To my mind, this puts historians in a similar position as the mathematicians found themselves about eleven months ago, when LLMs started to solve the first Erdős problems. Over the past year, we’ve watched these same models go from learning to read handwriting, to beginning to think historically, to mastering the undergraduate essay, and finally to making small but real contributions to human knowledge more or less autonomously. The trajectory seems clear.
